asks: What does the engine save of its own state?
answer: The state, and after it every input accepted since that save. This is a write-ahead log, the known practice. An input is written through to the disk before the core applies it. A new save is made when the inputs since the last one reach a fixed count, so the files have a fixed maximum size, and they are made at that size when the engine is set up, so that on a filesystem that writes in place a full disk does not stop a write to them. On a copy-on-write filesystem, such as APFS while the volume has a snapshot, an overwrite can still need new space; whether it does on a Mac is to find out, and a write that fails is handled as follows. A call whose write fails is refused with a named error and changes nothing. A driver result or a tick of the clock cannot be refused: when its write fails, the engine stops with a named failure, and at start it learns from the drivers what really exists, as `multi-step-operations` says. At start the engine loads the last saved state and applies the inputs after it, in order. The core is deterministic, so this gives the state it had, with the same events under the same numbers. Applying the inputs again issues no effect: what the drivers did is learned by reconciling at start. The saved state and each input carry a checksum and a format version. An input cut short at the end of the log was never accepted, and is dropped. Any other damage stops the start with a named failure: the engine does not guess a state. To find out: what it then starts from; what a newer engine does with an older format; and what the write costs per input on a Mac, and whether writes have to be grouped, which is measured.
